Fetch methods

Terminal demo
import sqlite3

conn = sqlite3.connect('my_database.db')
cursor = conn.cursor()
cursor.execute("SELECT id, first_name, last_name FROM employees WHERE department = 'IT'")
row = cursor.fetchone()
print(row)  # (2, 'Bob', 'Johnson')
Result shape
  • Rows are tuples by default, ordered like the SELECT clause.
  • Use fetchone to get a single tuple or None when exhausted.
  • Use fetchmany to process large sets in batches.
Key Takeaway

Fetch methods control memory and speed. Parameterized queries protect your data and users.

Common mistake

Don't build SQL with string concatenation; it opens SQL injection holes.

Pro tip

For big datasets, set cursor.arraysize then use fetchmany for predictable batches.

screens.title: Executing SELECT queries in Python
screens.narratorSegment: When you run a SELECT query from Python the usual pattern is to open a connection, create a cursor, and call the cursor's execute method with a S Q L string and optional parameters. The execute call sends the S Q L to the database engine, which prepares and runs the query, then the cursor becomes the handle for the resulting set of rows. Importantly, execute itself does not always return the rows; instead it readies the cursor so you can call fetch methods. A common example is selecting specific columns from an employees table. After execute, calling fetchone returns the next row, fetchall returns all remaining rows, and fetchmany returns a batch. A frequent misconception is expecting execute to return a Python list directly; DB-A P I separates execution from retrieval so you can choose the most efficient fetch pattern. Another important point is that some S Q L statements do not produce rows at all — CREATE TABLE or INSERT do not return result sets, so fetching after them will either be meaningless or raise an error. Practice by running a simple SELECT, observing the tuple structure, and then choosing the appropriate fetch method for your use case.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Executing SELECT
Definition

cursor.execute and result sets

Execute sends a SQL statement to the engine and prepares the cursor with any result set. Retrieval happens when you call fetch methods.

Explanation
  • execute does not always return rows directly; it prepares the cursor.
  • Only SELECT returns rows; DDL/DML usually do not produce result sets for fetching.
  • After execute, decide on fetchone/fetchall/fetchmany depending on size and needs.
Analogy
Think of execute as ordering food; fetch methods are the plates you choose to serve portions from the kitchen.
Concrete example
import sqlite3

conn = sqlite3.connect('my_database.db')
cursor = conn.cursor()
cursor.execute("SELECT id, first_name FROM employees WHERE department = 'IT'")
row = cursor.fetchone()
print(row)  # tuple or None
Key takeaway

Treat execution and retrieval as two steps: execute to prepare, then pick a fetch pattern that fits performance and memory constraints.

screens.title: Using cursor.fetchone()
screens.narratorSegment: cursor. fetchone retrieves the next row from the cursor's result set and returns it as a tuple, or returns None when there are no more rows. Use fetchone when you need to process rows sequentially and don’t want to hold the entire result set in memory. A common pattern is to call fetchone in a loop: fetch a row, check whether it is None, process it, and repeat. This pattern is simple and correct, but for very large datasets it can be slow due to many round-trips depending on driver buffering. An important misconception is assuming fetchone will return an empty tuple when finished — it returns None. Another practical tip: if you mix fetchone and fetchall on the same cursor without re-executing the query, remember that fetchall will only return remaining rows. Example: select IT employees and call fetchone twice to get two tuples, then None. Use fetchone for single-row needs like fetching a configuration entry by id, where memory impact is trivial and readability is high. For larger workloads, consider fetchmany instead to combine the benefits of batching and sequential processing.

keyIdea.text: fetchone returns the next row tuple or None when exhausted; it's ideal for sequential single-row processing and simple scripts.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › fetchone()
Definition

fetchone() behavior

fetchone returns the next row tuple or None when done. Use it where single-row handling or simple sequential processing is required.

  • Return value: tuple or None.
  • Good for configuration lookups or paged console output.
  • Not ideal if you need random access to all rows later.
Common mistake

Expecting an empty tuple instead of None leads to logic errors; always check is None to stop looping.

Example and usage
cursor.execute("SELECT id, first_name FROM employees WHERE department = 'IT'")
first = cursor.fetchone()
if first is not None:
  print(first)
second = cursor.fetchone()
if second is not None:
  print(second)
# Subsequent fetchone() returns None when finished
Key takeaway: Use fetchone for simple, readable sequential access and stop on None.

screens.title: Using cursor.fetchall()
screens.narratorSegment: cursor. fetchall returns all remaining rows from the cursor's result set as a list of tuples. This is convenient for small to medium result sets where you need to iterate multiple times or perform operations that require in-memory access, such as sorting or grouping in Python. However, fetchall loads everything into memory at once, so it can cause memory exhaustion for very large queries. A practical pattern is to use fetchall when you expect a reasonable number of rows, for example reading a small table of configuration items or a list of active users limited by a WHERE clause. Remember that fetchall returns an empty list if there are no rows, which is useful for conditional checks. A common mistake is always calling fetchall regardless of expected size — prefer fetchmany for large or unbounded results. If you call fetchone after fetchall on the same cursor without re-executing the query, there will be nothing left to fetch because fetchall consumed the result set. Use fetchall when convenience and simplicity outweigh memory concerns. Using cursor.fetchall() means fetchall loads remaining rows into a list of tuples — convenient but potentially memory-heavy for large datasets.. In practical terms, when to load all rows into memory and how to iterate them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › fetchall()

fetchall() — load all remaining rows

Use fetchall when you expect a bounded number of rows and want easy iteration. It returns a list of tuples or an empty list when there are no rows.

  • Good for small tables or when you need random access.
  • Returns [] when no rows remain, not None.
  • Avoid for hundreds of thousands of rows — memory warning.
Key takeaway

Choose fetchall only when the result size is known or small; otherwise prefer staged retrieval.

Example
cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM employees")
all_rows = cursor.fetchall()
if all_rows:
  for emp in all_rows:
    print(emp)
else:
  print("No employees found.")
Practical note: fetchall is helpful in scripts and tests, less so in production batch jobs that may return very large sets.

screens.title: Using cursor.fetchmany() and arraysize
screens.narratorSegment: fetchmany lets you retrieve a limited number of rows at a time, which is essential for processing very large result sets without exhausting memory. The method accepts a size argument; if omitted it uses cursor. arraysize, an attribute you can set to suggest a preferred batch size. A common pattern is to loop: call fetchmany until it returns an empty list, process each batch, and continue. This lets you read and handle thousands or millions of rows in predictable chunks. For example, set size to 1000 to process one thousand rows at a time and commit or write to disk between batches. A misconception is that fetchmany automatically pages results to disk; it still holds the batch in memory briefly, but the total memory footprint is limited by batch size. Also be mindful that different drivers may buffer rows differently, so arraysize is a hint, not a guarantee. Use fetchmany when you need a balance between the single-row simplicity of fetchone and the convenience of fetchall while keeping memory usage bounded. Using cursor.fetchmany() and arraysize means fetchmany returns a list of tuples in controlled batch sizes; use it to iterate large result sets without loading everything at once.. In practical terms, fetch rows in batches to control memory and throughput. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › fetchmany()
Process

Batch processing loop

  1. Execute the SELECT once to prepare the cursor.
  2. Call fetchmany(size=N) to get a list of up to N rows.
  3. If the list is empty, break; otherwise process the batch and repeat.
Why batches help
Batches limit peak memory, allow periodic commits, and give predictable performance characteristics for large exports or transformations.
Code example
cursor.execute("SELECT first_name, department FROM employees")
while True:
  batch = cursor.fetchmany(size=2)
  if not batch:
    break
  print(f"Processing batch of {len(batch)} rows")
  for row in batch:
    print(row)
Tip: set cursor.arraysize = 1000 before calling fetchmany to make it the default batch size.

screens.title: Tuple access vs. named access
screens.narratorSegment: By default DB-A P I drivers return rows as tuples where each element corresponds to a selected column by position. This is compact and fast, but can make code harder to read if you repeatedly use numeric indices like row[2] to get the hire date. Two common approaches address this: convert tuples to dictionaries yourself, or configure the driver to return row-like objects that support named access. For sqlite3 you can set conn. row_factory to sqlite3. Row before creating a cursor so rows behave like mappings and support access like row['first_name']. This improves readability and reduces index-related mistakes. A typical misconception is assuming you can use attribute access like row. first_name without configuring a row factory; that will not work by default. Use named access when code clarity and maintainability matter, and use tuples for micro-optimized hot paths where speed matters more than readability. If you need both, convert once at the boundary: fetch tuples and build dicts or named rows so the rest of your code uses clear keys, reducing indexing errors. Tuple access vs. named access means tuples are index-based and efficient; sqlite3.row enables named access for clearer, safer code.. In practical terms, understand index-based tuples and sqlite3.row named access. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Tuple vs Named

Index-based tuples

Fast and standard: each element maps to the SELECT order. But numeric indexing can be error-prone and less readable.

  • row[0] is the first selected column.
  • Best for small scripts or performance-critical loops.

Named access with sqlite3.Row

Set conn.row_factory = sqlite3.Row before creating a cursor to access columns by name like row['first_name']. This improves readability and reduces index errors.

conn = sqlite3.connect(db_file)
conn.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
cursor = conn.cursor()
cursor.execute("SELECT id, first_name FROM employees WHERE department = 'HR'")
emp = cursor.fetchone()
print(emp['first_name'])
Takeaway
Prefer named access for clarity in application code; use tuples when you must optimize inner loops.

screens.title: sqlite3.Row and named columns

This is especially useful when your SELECT clause uses many columns or the column order may change, because using a column name is clearer and less brittle. To use it, set the row_factory before creating any cursors, then call execute and fetch as usual. The row object supports mapping access like row['id'] and row['first_name'] which returns the value stored in that column. A common pitfall is setting row_factory after creating a cursor — it must be set before cursor creation. Another point to remember: sqlite3. Row still behaves like a lightweight object; if you need true dictionaries for serialization, convert rows explicitly. Use this pattern when you want readable code for printing or JSON conversion, and prefer tuples only when you need minimal overhead. Setup
conn = sqlite3.connect(db_file)
conn.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
cursor = conn.cursor()
Remember: set row_factory before creating the cursor or it will not take effect for that cursor.
Usage
cursor.execute("SELECT id, first_name FROM employees WHERE department = 'HR'")
row = cursor.fetchone()
if row:
  print(f"ID: {row['id']}, Name: {row['first_name']}")
Convert to a dict explicitly if you need JSON serialization: dict(row).

screens.title: Parameterized queries and SQL injection
screens.narratorSegment: Parameterized queries are the essential defense against S Q L injection. The core idea is simple: pass S Q L code and data separately to the driver so user-supplied values are treated as data only, never as executable S Q L. In sqlite3 the common placeholder is a question mark. For example, instead of building S Q L by concatenating user input into a string, pass the input as a second argument to cursor. execute. A dangerous practice is constructing queries with f-strings or string concatenation, which can let malicious input change the query structure. A common demonstration uses an input that includes S Q L punctuation to drop a table; this shows the damage possible when you don't parameterize. Parameterized queries instruct the driver to escape and bind values safely, preventing them from altering S Q L syntax. Remember that placeholder syntax varies by driver, so check your DB-A P I documentation. Also validate input for type and constraints even when you parameterize — parameterization prevents injection but not logical or semantic errors when wrong types are passed. Parameterized queries and SQL injection means always separate sql from data using parameterized queries; never build sql by concatenating user input.. In practical terms, why placeholders matter and how they stop injection. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Parameterized Queries

Danger vs Safe

Dangerous
user_input = "'; DROP TABLE products; --"
query = f"SELECT * FROM products WHERE name = '{user_input}'"
cursor.execute(query)
Safe pattern
search_name = 'Alice'
cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM employees WHERE first_name = ?", (search_name,))
# The value is bound safely by the driver
The driver handles escaping and binding; placeholders differ between drivers but the security principle is the same.
Takeaway
Parameterize all user data in SQL statements. Also validate data types and value ranges before sending them to the database.

screens.title: Safe parameterized queries in practice
screens.narratorSegment: A practical detail when using parameterized queries in sqlite3 is how to pass a single value as a parameter: you must supply a single-element tuple, which requires a trailing comma. For example, cursor. execute with a placeholder and (search_name,) ensures the driver receives a tuple, not a plain string. This small syntax rule is a common source of bugs for newcomers. Another useful pattern is to pass multiple parameters as a tuple in the same order as the placeholders in the S Q L string. Always match placeholders to values in count and order. Test your parameterized queries by trying both normal and malicious-looking inputs to confirm they are handled as data. Also remember that parameterization does not validate data types; if a number is required, validate it in Python before sending it. Practicing these syntactic details makes your code secure and reliable, and avoids embarrassments where queries fail due to incorrect parameter shapes rather than true logic errors. Safe parameterized queries in practice means use (value,) for single parameters and ensure placeholder count matches parameters to avoid runtime errors and keep queries safe.. Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Safe Parameter Use
Single-parameter syntax
search_name = 'Alice'
cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM employees WHERE first_name = ?", (search_name,))
# Note the trailing comma in the parameter tuple
If you pass the string directly without a tuple the driver may treat it differently, so always use a tuple or sequence.
Multiple parameters
cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM employees WHERE department = ? AND id >= ?", (dept, min_id))
Order of values must match placeholder order in SQL. This keeps the query deterministic and safe.
Common mistake
Forgetting the comma in a single-element tuple silently passes a string instead of a tuple, which usually triggers a parameter error at execution time.

screens.title: Context managers for connections
screens.narratorSegment: Using the with statement for database connections simplifies resource management dramatically. When you open a connection in a with block the connection is guaranteed to be closed when the block exits, and sqlite3's context manager will often commit if the block completes normally or roll back if an exception occurs. This reduces boilerplate try-except-finally code and prevents resource leaks. In practice you open a with sqlite3. connect(db_file) as conn, create a cursor inside, and run your execute and fetch calls inside the block. If you need to do multiple operations that must be atomic, the with block helps you keep commit and rollback behavior predictable. A common misconception is that with automatically commits every change without thought; while it often commits on normal exit, you should still call conn. commit after DML when explicit control is needed. For error handling, rely on the with behavior to rollback on exceptions and write small tests to confirm your driver’s exact semantics. Using with makes scripts and services simpler and safer. Context managers for connections means context managers ensure connections close and simplify commit/rollback handling, reducing error-prone boilerplate.. In practical terms, use with to open connections and ensure close/rollback semantics. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Context Managers

Using with for connections

with sqlite3.connect(db_file) as conn:
  cursor = conn.cursor()
  cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM products")
  rows = cursor.fetchall()
  # conn is closed automatically when the block ends
Note: call conn.commit explicitly for DML when you need deterministic timing of persistence.
Why use with
  • Automatic close and predictable cleanup.
  • Rollback on exception avoids partial commits.
  • Reduces boilerplate and improves readability.
Takeaway
Prefer with for concise, reliable connection and transaction management; test commit behavior per driver.

screens.title: Common mistakes and error handling
screens.narratorSegment: There are a few frequent errors you will encounter when querying from Python. First, trying to fetch after executing a DDL or DML statement that doesn't return rows is a logic error; fetchone and fetchall only make sense after SELECT. Second, mismatched parameter counts or wrong parameter types will raise errors at execute time — always ensure placeholder count matches the number of values and validate types beforehand. Third, forgetting to close connections can leak resources; this is why using with matters. Another common issue is assuming fetchall returns None for no rows; it returns an empty list. Likewise, fetchone returns None, not an empty tuple. Finally, poorly chosen batch sizes with fetchmany can either make your batches too small (causing extra overhead) or too large (defeating the point of batching). For robust code, catch sqlite3. Error exceptions, log the context, and let the context manager roll back transactions if something fails. Small tests that simulate no rows, many rows, and malformed input will reveal these edge cases quickly. Common mistakes and error handling means don't fetch after non-select statements, match parameter counts, use with to avoid leaks, and validate input before queries.. In practical terms, avoid fetching after dml and mismatched parameters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's recap the essential concepts you should carry forward. First, execute prepares a cursor-bound result set, and you must choose a fetch method—fetchone for single sequential rows, fetchall for small full loads, and fetchmany for controlled batching. Second, by default rows are tuples so access by numeric index maps to the SELECT order; use conn. row_factory = sqlite3. Row when you want named column access for clearer code. Third, parameterized queries are your guard against S Q L injection: always pass user data separately using placeholders appropriate for your driver. Fourth, use the with statement to manage connections automatically, ensuring close and consistent commit or rollback semantics. These four ideas cover correctness, performance, readability, and security when retrieving and processing data. Practice them in scripts and small tests to make them second nature. Which pattern will you use first in your projects: named rows for readability, or batch fetchmany for large exports?

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn how to run SELECT queries from Python and meaningfully process the rows the database returns. We'll cover the three primary fetch methods you will use every day, show how rows are represented by default, and explain safe parameterized queries that stop S Q L injection. You'll also see how the with statement makes connection handling cleaner and more reliable. For example, you'll practice selecting employees from a table, iterating through batches to avoid memory issues, and converting returned tuples to named-access rows when you need readable code. Knowing these patterns matters because retrieving data is the single most common database action in applications. A common misconception is that you can treat database results like in-memory objects immediately; instead, you must respect how the DB-A P I returns rows, when fetching is valid, and how drivers differ in placeholder syntax. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to fetch results efficiently, protect queries from injection, and write tidy connection code that is resilient to errors. Consider this your toolbox for safe, efficient querying.

Over the next screens you'll build four specific, verifiable skills. First, you'll execute SELECT queries from Python and interpret the returned rows so your code can make decisions based on real data. For example, you'll query an employees table and use the returned tuples to print names or update records. Second, you'll master fetchone, fetchall, and fetchmany so you can choose efficient retrieval patterns. You will learn when each method fits production code and how fetchmany prevents memory exhaustion with large result sets. Third, you'll implement parameterized queries to protect your application from S Q L injection; you'll see the dangerous pattern and the safe placeholder-based pattern and practice both. Fourth, you'll use the with statement as a context manager to manage connections and transactions reliably. This reduces boilerplate and guarantees connections close even if exceptions occur. Each objective ties to an explicit milestone so you can verify competency by running small scripts that show results and handle errors. These skills matter immediately: every app that reads a database relies on them for correctness, performance, and security.

This screen expands the objectives with concrete checks and examples you will run. First, when you execute a SELECT, you will check that the cursor returns a result set and use a small script to print the first returned tuple. A practical check is selecting employees in a department and printing their names. Second, for fetch methods you'll write three short snippets: one showing fetchone in a loop until None, one pulling all rows and counting them, and one using fetchmany with an explicit batch size to process rows in chunks. Third, for parameterized queries you'll intentionally contrast a dangerous string-concatenation example with a placeholder-based query. You will test both to observe behavior, and then explain why placeholders eliminate injection. Fourth, for context managers you'll convert a try-finally into a with block and observe that connections close and transactions commit or rollback automatically. Each check is short but targeted so you can prove competency quickly. These practical tests keep learning focused on usable outcomes rather than theory alone.

When you run a SELECT query from Python the usual pattern is to open a connection, create a cursor, and call the cursor's execute method with a S Q L string and optional parameters. The execute call sends the S Q L to the database engine, which prepares and runs the query, then the cursor becomes the handle for the resulting set of rows. Importantly, execute itself does not always return the rows; instead it readies the cursor so you can call fetch methods. A common example is selecting specific columns from an employees table. After execute, calling fetchone returns the next row, fetchall returns all remaining rows, and fetchmany returns a batch. A frequent misconception is expecting execute to return a Python list directly; DB-A P I separates execution from retrieval so you can choose the most efficient fetch pattern. Another important point is that some S Q L statements do not produce rows at all — CREATE TABLE or INSERT do not return result sets, so fetching after them will either be meaningless or raise an error. Practice by running a simple SELECT, observing the tuple structure, and then choosing the appropriate fetch method for your use case.

cursor. fetchone retrieves the next row from the cursor's result set and returns it as a tuple, or returns None when there are no more rows. Use fetchone when you need to process rows sequentially and don’t want to hold the entire result set in memory. A common pattern is to call fetchone in a loop: fetch a row, check whether it is None, process it, and repeat. This pattern is simple and correct, but for very large datasets it can be slow due to many round-trips depending on driver buffering. An important misconception is assuming fetchone will return an empty tuple when finished — it returns None. Another practical tip: if you mix fetchone and fetchall on the same cursor without re-executing the query, remember that fetchall will only return remaining rows. Example: select IT employees and call fetchone twice to get two tuples, then None. Use fetchone for single-row needs like fetching a configuration entry by id, where memory impact is trivial and readability is high. For larger workloads, consider fetchmany instead to combine the benefits of batching and sequential processing.

cursor. fetchall returns all remaining rows from the cursor's result set as a list of tuples. This is convenient for small to medium result sets where you need to iterate multiple times or perform operations that require in-memory access, such as sorting or grouping in Python. However, fetchall loads everything into memory at once, so it can cause memory exhaustion for very large queries. A practical pattern is to use fetchall when you expect a reasonable number of rows, for example reading a small table of configuration items or a list of active users limited by a WHERE clause. Remember that fetchall returns an empty list if there are no rows, which is useful for conditional checks. A common mistake is always calling fetchall regardless of expected size — prefer fetchmany for large or unbounded results. If you call fetchone after fetchall on the same cursor without re-executing the query, there will be nothing left to fetch because fetchall consumed the result set. Use fetchall when convenience and simplicity outweigh memory concerns. Using cursor.fetchall() means fetchall loads remaining rows into a list of tuples — convenient but potentially memory-heavy for large datasets.. In practical terms, when to load all rows into memory and how to iterate them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

fetchmany lets you retrieve a limited number of rows at a time, which is essential for processing very large result sets without exhausting memory. The method accepts a size argument; if omitted it uses cursor. arraysize, an attribute you can set to suggest a preferred batch size. A common pattern is to loop: call fetchmany until it returns an empty list, process each batch, and continue. This lets you read and handle thousands or millions of rows in predictable chunks. For example, set size to 1000 to process one thousand rows at a time and commit or write to disk between batches. A misconception is that fetchmany automatically pages results to disk; it still holds the batch in memory briefly, but the total memory footprint is limited by batch size. Also be mindful that different drivers may buffer rows differently, so arraysize is a hint, not a guarantee. Use fetchmany when you need a balance between the single-row simplicity of fetchone and the convenience of fetchall while keeping memory usage bounded. Using cursor.fetchmany() and arraysize means fetchmany returns a list of tuples in controlled batch sizes; use it to iterate large result sets without loading everything at once.. In practical terms, fetch rows in batches to control memory and throughput. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

By default DB-A P I drivers return rows as tuples where each element corresponds to a selected column by position. This is compact and fast, but can make code harder to read if you repeatedly use numeric indices like row[2] to get the hire date. Two common approaches address this: convert tuples to dictionaries yourself, or configure the driver to return row-like objects that support named access. For sqlite3 you can set conn. row_factory to sqlite3. Row before creating a cursor so rows behave like mappings and support access like row['first_name']. This improves readability and reduces index-related mistakes. A typical misconception is assuming you can use attribute access like row. first_name without configuring a row factory; that will not work by default. Use named access when code clarity and maintainability matter, and use tuples for micro-optimized hot paths where speed matters more than readability. If you need both, convert once at the boundary: fetch tuples and build dicts or named rows so the rest of your code uses clear keys, reducing indexing errors. Tuple access vs. named access means tuples are index-based and efficient; sqlite3.row enables named access for clearer, safer code.. Using the with statement for database connections simplifies resource management dramatically. When you open a connection in a with block the connection is guaranteed to be closed when the block exits, and sqlite3's context manager will often commit if the block completes normally or roll back if an exception occurs. This reduces boilerplate try-except-finally code and prevents resource leaks. In practice you open a with sqlite3. connect(db_file) as conn, create a cursor inside, and run your execute and fetch calls inside the block. If you need to do multiple operations that must be atomic, the with block helps you keep commit and rollback behavior predictable. A common misconception is that with automatically commits every change without thought; while it often commits on normal exit, you should still call conn. commit after DML when explicit control is needed.
